articles.title: Nearly 7 in 10 professors report being bullied, often by students over grades
articles.author: Jason Walker, Associate Professor of Psychology, Health and Wellness, Adler University
articles.summary: The rates are similar to high-stress workplaces like emergency services.
articles.contentHtml:
Faculty and university staff members report being bullied in two ways: by their colleagues and supervisors, and by their students over grades, according to an international study I conducted with colleagues Zahra Moradi and Deborah Circo.

Researchers define workplace bullying as harmful acts of mistreatment between people that go beyond incivility and cross the line to intentionally cause harm. In other words, it’s behavior any reasonable person would know isn’t OK.

Junior faculty and staff faced more workplace bullying from peers. Faculty members and staff who are Black, Indigenous or people of color were targeted more frequently.

Senior faculty were more likely than younger educators to report being bullied by students over grades. Although bullying usually runs down the chain of power – for example, from a boss to an employee – grade bullying flips that. Researchers call it contrapower harassment – when someone with less formal power targets someone with more.

More than 30% of adult workers in the U.S. and Canada experience bullying, harassment and sexual abuse in the workplace at any given time, harming both individuals and organizations.

That rate is more than double in academia, where bullying rates are as high as 68% at some institutions, far exceeding those in general workplaces and aligning with high-stress fields like emergency services, according to our peer-reviewed findings published in the October 2026 Journal of Multidisciplinary Research and Practice.

Why it matters

Academic bullying undermines both the well-being of staff and faculty and the integrity of higher education institutions.

Thirty percent of our survey respondents reported that students pressured them for a better grade. Students’ tactics included threatening grade appeals, malicious complaints, negative online reviews, emotional manipulation and intimidation. Women and minority faculty are particularly affected. Over time, the bullying creates a toxic environment that damages relationships between faculty and students and hurts the quality of education for everyone.

Such pressure could result in mental health issues like anxiety and depression, decreased job satisfaction and reduced productivity. These dynamics not only affect individual faculty members but can also lead to long-term damage to the reputation of institutions and negatively impact students’ educational experiences.

How we did our work

We surveyed 189 faculty and staff at colleges and universities in Canada, the U.S. and U.K.

Anonymous respondents reported how often they’d faced 22 common forms of mistreatment from colleagues and supervisors. A separate set of questions asked about pressure from students over grades.

The most common issues related to colleagues weren’t shouting or threats. They were easier to dismiss: unmanageable workloads, withheld information and impossible deadlines.

Pressure from students over grades was reported more frequently than bullying from colleagues.

What still isn’t known

Gaps remain in understanding the root causes of bullying of faculty.

Studies that follow the same faculty over several years could show how grade bullying builds over time, and whether it pushes people to leave or lose trust in their institutions. One likely pattern is that grade bullying escalates when it works, wearing faculty down until they either give in or leave their jobs.

Researchers need to test what actually works to stop bullying, and whether those fixes hold up at different kinds of colleges and universities.

Bigger studies would help. So would sitting down with faculty and hearing their experiences in their own words to add context that a survey can’t capture.

Future research could also explore interventions to mitigate bullying and measure their effectiveness across diverse educational contexts.

Bullying at work is a form of violence. The harm is psychological rather than physical, but it’s real. Change starts with higher standards of conduct for everyone, from first-year students to senior administrators and leaders committed to enforcing respectful rules.

The Research Brief is a short take on interesting academic work.

articles.title: How your body clock affects your mental health and ways to keep it in sync
articles.author: Sarah Chellappa, Associate Professor, Cognitive and Affective Neuroscience, University of Southampton
articles.summary: Research shows that disrupted body clocks can affect mood. A circadian rhythms researcher explains how sleep, light and meal timing influence mental health.
articles.contentHtml:
Ever wondered why a bad night’s sleep can leave you irritable, anxious or sad? Poor sleep affects our emotions, but its timing also plays a role.

Our circadian rhythms are nearly 24-hour cycles that regulate alertness, hormones, body temperature and digestion.

Deep inside the brain, a cluster of nerve cells called the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) acts as the body’s master clock. It uses light signals from the eyes to coordinate clocks in other organs, including the brain, liver, heart and gut.

When daily routines fall out of sync with this clock, mood can suffer. Research suggests circadian disruption may contribute to mental health challenges.

Our internal clock helps regulate hormones, including melatonin and cortisol. Melatonin helps regulate the sleep-wake cycle. Levels stay low during the day, rise in the evening as darkness falls (signalling to the brain that it is time to rest), peak in the middle of the night, and drop off in the morning. Cortisol, which helps us respond to stress, typically rises towards morning.

These changes prepare the body for activity and rest, while influencing emotional wellbeing.

In a 2024 laboratory study, my colleagues and I investigated whether our internal clocks influence mood independently of everyday activities.

We studied 19 healthy adults over 32 hours, measuring mood while minimising changes in their surroundings and behaviour.

We found that anxiety-like and depression-like mood were highest at around 8am to 9am, while participants reported greater mental fatigue and lower physical comfort between approximately 6am and 8am. These patterns were linked to their internal biological clocks, suggesting that mood can fluctuate according to biological time, independently of everyday routines.

Circadian disruption has also been linked to depression and bipolar disorder, a condition involving episodes of depression and elevated or irritable mood.

The relationship also works in both directions. Mental health difficulties can disrupt sleep and circadian rhythms, potentially creating a cycle in which low quality sleep and psychological distress reinforce one another.

What happens when our clocks fall out of sync

Night shift workers may need to stay awake when their bodies are preparing for sleep and rest when their internal clocks promote alertness.

This mismatch is known as circadian misalignment.

In a 2020 study, we investigated how this misalignment affected mood in two controlled laboratory experiments involving people with and without shift-work experience.

Participants followed schedules designed to simulate day and night shifts while all other behavioural and environmental factors were controlled for, including light exposure, physical activity, food intake and opportunities for sleep.

We found that mood and wellbeing reduced when participants’ sleeping and waking schedules were misaligned with their internal body clock. The effects were observed in non-shift workers as well as shift workers.

These findings suggest circadian misalignment can influence mood, although larger studies are needed to establish the long-term consequences.

Outside the laboratory, many people experience a mismatch known as social jetlag. This occurs when people’s sleep and waking times differ substantially between working days and days off.

Artificial light can also affect our internal clocks. Bright light in the evening, including light from electronic screens, can suppress melatonin and delay our sleep time.

My research on light sensitivity has highlighted differences between individuals. Some people’s circadian rhythms are much more sensitive to evening light than others, meaning the same exposure may have different effects.

Could changing meal times help?

Light is the strongest environmental signal for the master clock, but eating also influences the timing of biological processes in other organs.

In a 2022 study, my colleagues and I investigated whether changing meal times could reduce the effects of simulated night work on mood.

Nineteen healthy volunteers followed carefully controlled schedules designed to mimic night shifts. One group ate during both the day and night, while the other ate only during the daytime.

Among participants who ate during both periods, ratings of depression-like mood increased by 26.2% and anxiety-like mood by 16.1% compared with their baseline measurements.

We did not observe significant increases in either measure among those who ate only during the daytime.

These findings suggest that the timing of meals may influence how circadian disruption affects mood. However, the study involved a small group of healthy volunteers under laboratory conditions. Further research involving shift workers is needed to establish whether eating only during the daytime can help reduce symptoms of anxiety and depression.

How to support your body clock

Although we may not control our working hours or sleep schedules, some daily habits may help keep our internal clocks aligned.

  1. Get morning daylight. Light is the most powerful environmental signal for the master clock. Spending time outdoors after waking can support alertness and help regulate the timing of sleep later. The amount of light needed varies between people.

Read more: Tired, irritable and craving carbs? Why darker days affect our bodies and brains

  1. Reduce bright light before bed. Dimming household lights and limiting screen use in the evening/night-time may help the body prepare for sleep. The NHS recommends avoiding electronic screens for at least an hour before bedtime.

  2. Keep a regular sleep-wake schedule. Going to bed and waking up at reasonably consistent times can help reinforce circadian rhythms. A systematic review associated regular sleep patterns with better health outcomes, including diabetes, heart diseases and depression.

  3. Consider food and exercise timing. Consistent and earlier food times may help support the body’s daily rhythms for physical health, although research is needed to establish the best eating schedules for mental health. Regular physical activity can also benefit sleep. A review of studies found that evening exercise generally did not interfere with sleep, although vigorous exercise ending very close to bedtime sometimes did.

Protecting sleep and mental health

Research suggests that the timing of sleep and daily activities can influence mood, although more evidence is needed to establish whether changing these routines can help prevent or treat mental health conditions.

Maintaining consistent routines and getting enough sleep may support emotional wellbeing, but these habits cannot replace appropriate treatment. Anyone experiencing persistent sleep or mood problems should seek medical advice. Understanding how our internal clocks influence mood may eventually offer new ways to support mental health.

Sarah Chellappa does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

articles.title: Can creatine help your mental health? Here’s what the latest evidence says
articles.author: Zudin Puthucheary, Professor of Intensive Care Medicine, Queen Mary University of London
articles.summary: The brain needs a lot of energy. Without a sufficient supply, mood and mental health may be affected.
articles.contentHtml:
Once a supplement favoured mainly by fitness fanatics, creatine has quickly become one of the most widely used dietary add-ons in the world.

While its advantages for strength and athletic performance are supported by evidence, it’s increasingly being recommended for its mental health effects. In fact, a recent review has even suggested the supplement may have benefits as a treatment for depression.

There are many reasons why creatine appears to be beneficial for our brains and mental health. But before you start taking the supplement for your wellbeing, it’s important to understand the nuance of what the research has found so far.

Creatine is a compound that our bodies naturally make. It’s also found in meat (both white and red) and some fish (including salmon, tuna, cod and herring).

Creatine acts as a source of energy in the body. It primarily helps deliver energy to our muscles when we’re active. Most of our creatine is stored in our muscles, with small amounts also stored in the brain.

The brain is one of the most energy-hungry organs in the body. Although it only accounts for 2% of our total body weight, it uses 20% of the body’s energy – especially during complex thinking and tasks.

When energy is low in the brain, it can affect the important chemicals that control mood. Low brain energy is also thought to contribute to different types of mental health issues, including depression, bipolar disorder and schizophrenia. Research also found that people who are depressed can have low levels of creatine in the front of their brains, a key area associated with mood.

This is why it has been suggested that creatine may be useful for treating mental health conditions, including depression.

Depression and creatine

Forty years ago, scientists found a relationship between having suicidal thoughts and low creatine levels.

Since then, numerous studies have investigated whether there’s a link between creatine levels and mental health.

Large studies have found that people who consume more creatine have lower rates of depression.

Research has also found that teenagers with treatment-resistant depression who took creatine supplements alongside their usual medication found their mood improved. The same was true in people with bipolar disorder, who reported that using a creatine supplement alongside their normal medication improved symptoms.

To get a better overview of what benefit creatine has on mental health, a recent systematic review was conducted. They looked at five trials and 238 patients. Two of the trials showed a benefit; three did not.

However, it’s important to note that each of these trials was small, and they all tested different questions. For instance, some tested creatine by itself, some tested whether taking creatine alongside antidepressants had an effect, and others tested whether taking creatine alongside psychotherapy had benefits.

The doses of creatine and the amount of time people took the supplement also varied significantly. This makes it hard to draw a firm conclusion, so better trials are needed.

Creatine and brain health

Researchers are also investigating whether creatine can benefit other areas of cognitive health – particularly those related to memory.

Our brain’s ability to process and use information is highly energy dependent. If that energy supply is disrupted, it can affect how we process and remember information.

For instance, sleep deprivation is known to affect many aspects of cognitive function – including attention and memory processing. Research points to a lack of brain energy as a potential explanation.

Studies scanning human brains have found that in people who are sleep deprived, the brain uses more creatine. This can affect how much available creatine is stored in the body.

Research has also found that topping up creatine stores after a bad night’s sleep could counteract the effects of sleep deprivation on the brain.

A study of 15 healthy people explored the effect of taking a single, high dose of creatine (around 25g) on sleep deprivation and cognitive function. Brain scans of the participants showed that sleep deprivation had decreased brain creatine stores. But when they took the creatine, the scans showed it was used by the brain.

The participants who took the creatine also saw improvements on short-term memory tasks, reaction speed and information processing compared to the group who did not receive creatine.

This small study is not enough proof to recommend creatine for sleep deprivation. But considering that sleep deprivation is also linked to increased risk of anxiety and depression, this could be a useful, short-term strategy for looking after cognitive health.

Because brain energy affects so many things, there’s also interest in what effects it might have on other brain diseases.

Impaired brain energy is considered an important factor in the progression of Alzheimer’s disease. Many parts of the brain affected by Alzheimer’s also appear to have low creatine levels.

Only one very small study has investigated this link. Although the study found creatine had encouraging effects on fluid intelligence (ability to think abstractly and reason quickly), reading and working memory in patients with Alzheimer’s disease, more research is needed before it can be recommended as a treatment.

It’s important to note that all of the studies that have explored creatine’s benefits for mental health or cognitive health have been quite small – so there’s no conclusive scientific evidence yet.

We also don’t know the right dose or how long to take it for. It may be that a person needs to take a higher creatine dose and for a longer period than they would if they were just taking it for fitness. This is because creatine doesn’t transport easily into the brain. It will be important to understand which dose is right for the brain, and whether that dosage is still safe.

For now, the best thing to do is to ensure you eat enough creatine as part of a balanced diet.

Zudin Puthucheary is affiliated with the Intensive Care Society and the National Confidential Enquiry into Patient Outcome and Death.

articles.title: France: three overlapping woes are fuelling a generation of discontent
articles.author: Jean-Philippe Bouilloud, Professeur d’organisation et de sociologie des sciences, ESCP Business School
articles.summary: The anxiety overload at the root of widespread high school closures and protest action explains parents’ show of support for the youth-led movement.
articles.contentHtml:
KEY TAKEAWAYS

  • The French high schooler-led uprising is not a sign of a generational struggle pitting the young against baby boomers.

  • The uprisings indicate a state of discontentment reflecting three grievances: failings within the education system, eco-anxiety and concerns over employment in the age of AI.

  • Far from demanding a break with the established order, young protesters are simply asking for the right to live a good and fair life… like their predecessors before them.

Rarely has Freud’s Civilization and Its Discontents seemed so relevant to the times in which we are living. Although the discontents we are currently witnessing do not necessarily affect society as a whole, they are certainly impacting an entire generation born in the 21st century, as well as their parents and their social environment. Admittedly, we know that generations are not homogeneous and that any attempt to generalise is an oversimplification. Nevertheless, the high schoolers that are taking to the streets to protest in this day and age belong to a relatively homogeneous age cohort.

You would be forgiven for thinking that the current unrest is the result of a clash of generations. From the outside, it is often viewed as a generational tug of war between a struggling young population and the rest: an aging but relatively prosperous Europe. Criticism is, without doubt, being directed at “baby-boomers” or those born during the thirty years following World War II (which were marked by economic prosperity and low unemployment, conditions that now seem a world away today).

The problem lies elsewhere

Nevertheless, this is not a generational conflict, and the fact that a substantial proportion of parents, as well as the majority of the population, share the students’ demands shows that the problem lies elsewhere. These demands are nothing new, and they help explain why many parents joined their children during the first demonstrations, along with teachers, to show their support over deteriorating conditions in high schools.

The students and their initial demands were hijacked by more politically radical movements, some even revolutionary or anarchist, as well as opportunistic groups that took advantage of the disorder to loot shops and businesses, without any tangible political agenda. According to an official report dated October 14, 2026, “937 law enforcement officers, 248 students and 149 members of educational staff have been injured since the beginning of the high school student movement.” The demonstrations on October 18 resulted in more than 1,800 arrests. The proliferation of various groups with overlapping demands muddles the student movements’ original message, leaving us with little more than the smouldering remnants of a battlefield. Nevertheless, it is the central concerns of these students that I wish to explore here. Ultimately, this movement appears to lie at the intersection of several anxiety-inducing issues. Rather than speaking of a convergence of struggles, we should speak of a convergence of anxieties.

Three sources of anxiety

The movement appears to reflect the convergence of three factors that are also sources of concern:

  • the perceived deterioration of public education

  • ecological anxiety

  • the new difficulties young people face in the labour market, particularly those associated with the development of artificial intelligence (AI).

These three factors provide fertile ground for psychosocial anxiety.

The high school students’ main demands appear legitimate and concern improving working conditions: replacing absent teachers, shortening excessively long school days, reducing the number of students per class, repairing and maintaining infrastructure, and improving or abolishing Parcoursup, the widely criticised higher education admissions platform that is often difficult to understand.

These demands echo the broader perception that conditions in the French school system have deteriorated and that the system is relatively inefficient compared with those of neighbouring countries. This is confirmed year after year by the PISA survey: over a period of 25 years, France has fallen from 12th to 29th place in the overall rankings, with declining performance in every area measured: reading, mathematics, and science. Admittedly, the number of countries participating in the survey has increased, but the scores themselves clearly demonstrate a deterioration in student performance, in a context in which results across OECD countries have been stagnating for several years.

Yet this is not due to a lack of time spent in the classroom. French high school students spend 34 hours a week in class, compared with 18.8 hours in Finland, whose students achieve considerably better results than their French counterparts (Finland ranks 12th overall, compared with France in 29th place). The traditional French ideal of a free, public, and compulsory education system rested on the basic assumption that the quality of its teaching would lead to a future in which good academic results would be rewarded.

Today, however, confidence in the education system has eroded considerably, and no favourable alternative has emerged. As the French sociologist François Dubet aptly puts it,

“There is no future outside school, and school cannot guarantee any future.”

Combined with a sense of social injustice experienced in many disadvantaged neighbourhoods, this exasperation at the decline of what is perceived as the only avenue for social mobility is seen as a betrayal of France’s republican ideal.

The relatively new phenomenon of widespread eco-anxiety, is also another underlying issue which appears to be affecting a significant proportion of young people. In 2025, the French Agency for Ecological Transition (ADEME), a highly respected public agency, estimated that “16.6 million French people exhibit symptoms of psychological distress related to the environment,” a phenomenon that appears to affect young people and those aged 25–34, in particular. The unusually hot summer we have just experienced is hardly likely to alleviate these anxieties. In much public discourse, global warming is largely attributed to the postwar capitalist production system. The convergence of these educational and ecological concerns is illustrated, for example, by the highly publicised visit of Swedish activist Greta Thunberg to show her support at a high school in the Paris region.

Against this already bleak backdrop, concerns about unemployment have recently emerged as well, since young people aged 15–24 are the group most affected by unemployment, with a rate of 19.8%, compared with a national average of 7.7%. The new reality of AI adds another dimension, echoing the much criticised Parcoursup algorithm and giving rise to a new and augmented form of digital anxiety, this time by calling into question the promise of future employment. Thus, faced with a university system that no longer delivers on its promises and an increasingly degraded ecological environment, young people find that the world of work itself is slipping out of their reach…

A desire to take control of their destiny and live a decent life

Interviews with high school students, along with their stated demands, regularly reveal a desire to be heard and to have “a say in the matter”. These demonstrations can be understood as an expression of the desire to take control of one’s own destiny and to be insoumis or unbowed or unwilling to submit a term borrowed from the name of France’s far left political party (La France insoumise) that has become increasingly popular among young people. A changing social and economic landscape is perceived to be going in the wrong direction and governed by out-of-touch older generations whose track record to date undermines their legitimacy to govern.

Let us hypothesise that, in a social space permeated by social media, occupying educational institutions serves two purposes: it provides an opportunity, however briefly and even if only in an illusory way, to reclaim spaces dedicated to learning and everyday work, and it also makes it possible to forge genuine social bonds. In contrast to the “linear time” of everyday life, which scatters individuals behind their screens, social media plays the role of an intermediary institution between the individual and society. This civil uprising provides an opportunity to put human relationships at the centre, and reaffirm solidarity in numbers, i.e. groups, which come together in this way to challenge the established order and vent its woes. Such movements have an element of “celebration” to them, which can be seen in the humour displayed on many protest banners and in the music accompanying the marches. But, as French sociologist Roger Caillois already reminded us in the Man and the Sacred (1939), modern celebration can also take the form of war, like group affirmation via violent outbreaks…

The uprisings in France bring together anxieties that extend beyond the high schoolers’ realm and concern the world of work in the broadest sense. Once again, the students who took part in the initial demonstrations are not fighting to work less, but to be able to do meaningful and satisfying work under satisfactory conditions, in other words, to have a good and fair life.

Thanks to MM Gabriel Lomellini and Magwyer Grimes for their comments on this article.

articles.title: Autistic children come to A&E in mental health crisis from as young as eight
articles.author: Emma Ashworth, Associate Professor in Child & Adolescent Mental Health, Liverpool John Moores University
articles.summary: The data showed autistic children were seeking help for suicidal thoughts in A&E at significantly younger ages than their non-autistic peers.
articles.contentHtml:
Research consistently shows that autistic people face higher risks of mental health difficulties and are more likely to think about or attempt suicide than the general population.

For example, a 2014 study found that up to 66% of those surveyed had had suicidal thoughts (compared to 20% of non-autistic adults) and up to 35% have planned or attempted suicide. There may be many reasons for this, but it is thought that pressures such as chronic stress, isolation and bullying, compounded by trauma, anxiety and inadequate support, can lead to exhaustion and hopelessness.

We need to find ways to intervene earlier with autistic young people, to build wellbeing, prevent crisis and create safer environments around them.

To help us do this, we need to look at the experiences of autistic children across education, health and social care services. This includes A&E, where past studies have shown that autistic children are nine times more likely to receive psychiatric care than non-autistic children.

Our study – a collaboration between researchers at Liverpool John Moores University, children’s mental health charity Anna Freud, Edge Hill University, University College London and Alder Hey Children’s NHS Foundation Trust – set out to map patterns among young people in suicidal crisis at A&E. We analysed the records of 338 young people aged eight to 16 who attended a UK paediatric hospital A&E for suicidal crisis over three years.

Patterns within emergency departments

We found that autistic young people were disproportionately represented, at over a third (35.8%) of all attendees. Nearly two thirds of these (62%) were girls. This mirrors the way autistic girls are often under-identified in childhood, leading to missed or late diagnosis and more internalising difficulties. This can result in an increased risk of anxiety, depression and suicidality.

The data showed autistic children were seeking help for suicidal thoughts in A&E at significantly younger ages than their non-autistic peers (eight v ten years). This could suggest that the cumulative emotional toll of negative experiences builds up faster or starts earlier for autistic children. It’s consistent with previous research which found that negative school experiences generate twice the emotional burden in autistic and ADHD adolescents compared to their neurotypical classmates.

We found that autistic young people were more likely to have a pre-existing mental health diagnosis (64% v 46%). They were also more likely to have previously been seen by Child and Adolescent Mental Health Services (CAMHS)(74% v 49%) and to have repeat A&E attendances for suicidal crisis (31% v 18%).

This highlights a paradox: autistic young people were more likely to be known to CAMHS and to have sought help at A&E previously, but were also more likely than non-autistic young people to attend (and re-attend) A&E in suicidal crisis. This points to a gap between recognising an autistic child is struggling and delivering the help they need, with A&E departments left to act as a safety net when earlier support falls short.

What can services learn?

As this was a single-site UK study based on routine clinical records (which can be incomplete), we may not be able to generalise the findings to other settings. Despite this, we think these findings have implications for how to provide earlier and better care.

CAMHS are incredibly stretched. Limited resources means the threshold to receive help is very high, with many not getting support as a result. Barriers are even steeper for autistic young people. For example, “diagnostic overshadowing”, where symptoms of mental health difficulties are attributed to autism, is common. Furthermore, some therapeutic options aren’t suited to how autistic people think and communicate. Improving the accessibility of services and offering adapted support could help reduce the risk of crisis.

Alternatives to A&E are also needed. The government’s recent announcement of 159 new NHS mental health centres in England will help provide crisis care in the community. However, crisis alternatives tailored to the needs of autistic people still need to be developed and delivered, to offer more appropriate pathways specifically for autistic young people. Improved early intervention in schools and communities can also support prevention.

The A&E environment is likely also part of the problem, with bright lights, noise and unpredictability intensifying overwhelm. This can make it harder to assess a young autistic person and more likely they’ll leave before being seen. Small changes like quiet rooms and ear defenders could help.

Communication differences can further complicate A&E experiences for autistic people. Expressing distress non-verbally may increase the risk of crisis being misread, missed or misunderstood, particularly in such a busy environment. Tools like communication passports and reasonable-adjustment flags are starting to appear in some NHS services but could be made standard practice.

These changes are not possible without services being given adequate funding and resources. Staff training in autism is also key, with the NHS-funded National Autism Trainer Programme providing a good model.

Our findings show that something isn’t working in services for a group of children at serious risk of harm. In collaboration with autistic young people and their families, we need to turn this evidence into action, providing much earlier support and building safer, more understanding environments so that no one falls through the gaps.

Emma Ashworth received funding from Liverpool John Moores University QR Policy Support Fund to conduct the research associated with this article.

Georgia Pavlopoulou has an honorary contract with mental health charity Anna Freud. She is Chair of Autism Central, England's Autism Peer Education Programme.

articles.title: How the body clock could help personalise depression treatment
articles.author: Timothy Hearn, Lecturer, University of Cambridge; Anglia Ruskin University
articles.summary: A new study suggests that sleep patterns may be linked to how people respond to antidepressants, raising the possibility of more personalised treatment.
articles.contentHtml:
A person with depression might sleep much longer than usual and still wake feeling exhausted. Later that evening, when they want to go to bed, they may find themselves wide awake. Researchers are investigating whether patterns like these could help explain why antidepressants work better for some people than others.

The clue may lie in the body’s internal clock, which helps regulate when someone sleeps, wakes and feels alert.

An Australian study examined 11,380 people, predominantly with severe or recurring depression. About 23% met the researchers’ criteria for a proposed subtype called “circadian depression”, named after the body’s roughly 24-hour internal clock.

Participants needed at least three of six features, including being a night owl, sleeping longer during depression, morning tiredness and seasonal changes in mood or behaviour. The other features involved habitually sleeping and waking later, and having different sleep schedules on working days and days off.

Compared with other participants, this group reported less benefit and more side-effects from two common types of antidepressants, SSRIs and SNRIs, which affect how brain cells communicate through chemical messengers. However, some people with these sleep patterns still reported benefiting from these medicines.

The researchers also found genetic associations with later sleep timing, reduced sensitivity to insulin, the hormone that helps regulate blood sugar, and a protein involved in inflammation, the immune system’s response to injury or infection. These associations reflect inherited tendencies, rather than evidence that participants actually had blood-sugar problems or inflammation.

The findings are preliminary. Participants recalled their symptoms and medication experiences, and those in the proposed group generally had more severe depression. The researchers did not measure their internal clocks or establish cause and effect.

Some features overlap with recognised forms of depression, so it remains unclear whether this is a distinct subtype. All participants had European genetic ancestry, limiting how widely the findings can be applied. The 23% figure therefore cannot be assumed to represent everyone with depression.

How the body clock affects mood

The body clock coordinates roughly 24-hour cycles, known as circadian rhythms, which affect sleepiness, body temperature and hormones, the chemical messengers that help regulate the body. Light reaching the eyes helps keep this clock aligned with day and night. Meals and physical activity also provide timing cues.

When internal timing clashes with daily demands, sleep can suffer. Someone whose clock runs late may feel alert at midnight but have to get up for work while their body is still expecting sleep. Being a night owl is not necessarily a problem. Persistent disruption is the concern.

Sleep and mental health can reinforce one another. Disrupted sleep may worsen depression, while depression and stress can disturb sleep and daily routines.

One possible link involves brain systems that regulate emotion and reward, including the ability to enjoy pleasurable experiences. Animal experiments suggest that disrupting the body clock can affect these systems and produce depression-like behaviour.

In small laboratory experiments, researchers altered the sleep schedules of shift workers and people who did not work shifts. When their sleep and waking times were out of step with their internal clocks, participants reported worse mood. They had not been recruited because they had depression, and temporary low mood is different from clinical depression.

Conventional antidepressants might leave a timing problem untreated, but that remains a hypothesis. The Australian study did not test body-clock treatments, and its findings cannot establish whether someone with disrupted rhythms would benefit more from an alternative medication.

Could light therapy help?

Light therapy involves sitting near a specially designed bright-light box at a scheduled time, often in the morning. Morning light can shift a late-running body clock earlier, helping someone feel sleepy and wake earlier.

Read more: Why morning blue light therapy could improve sleep and daily activity in older adults

The treatment is used for seasonal affective disorder, depression that follows a seasonal pattern, often during darker months. Evidence suggests it can also help with depression that has no seasonal pattern.

A review of 11 clinical trials involving 858 people examined bright-light therapy for non-seasonal depression, including bipolar depression. Bipolar disorder involves depression alongside episodes of unusually elevated or irritable mood and increased energy.

In trials reporting remission, about 41% of people receiving bright light improved enough to fall below the threshold for depression, compared with 24% receiving dim light or treatment without bright light.

But these trials did not select people with the proposed circadian subtype, so they cannot tell us whether that group benefits more. Light may also influence mood through brain pathways separate from the body clock.

Timing and medical guidance matter. Light can shift the clock earlier or later depending on when it is used. People with bipolar disorder need particular supervision because light therapy can sometimes trigger unusually elevated or irritable mood.

Regular waking times, daytime activity and meals may also support daily rhythms. Melatonin, a hormone that rises in the evening and signals biological night, can help shift a delayed clock when carefully timed. However, studies have not established melatonin supplements as an effective depression treatment.

Towards more personalised treatment

Could measuring someone’s internal clock help doctors choose treatments? Wrist-worn activity monitors can estimate sleep patterns, while saliva samples taken throughout an evening can show when melatonin starts rising, offering a more direct measure of internal timing.

Researchers need to establish whether the proposed group really has distinct biological rhythms, then test whether choosing treatment based on those measurements helps people recover sooner.

For now, sleep patterns cannot reliably predict which antidepressant will work best, and the findings provide no reason to change prescribed medication without medical advice.

If future trials confirm a benefit, a prescription for depression might one day specify when to receive light as carefully as which medicine to take.

articles.title: Spending in-person time with friends is the biggest predictor of whether college students flourish
articles.author: Roxanne Prichard, Professor of Psychology, University of St. Thomas
articles.summary: Helping young people thrive involves supporting healthy relationships, as well as being engaged in work, school and family life.
articles.contentHtml:
Exercise, avoiding alcohol or even getting enough sleep aren’t the factors most connected to college students’ well-being.

Spending face-to-face time with friends and other people is the strongest predictor of their mental health, according to a 2026 study of nearly 80,000 students that I conducted with the help of my students.

This finding matters because young people are spending less time together in person and more time communicating through screens.

Between 2010 and 2022, the percentage of U.S. high school seniors who reported seeing friends face-to-face almost every day declined from 44% to 32%.

Against this backdrop, mental health challenges among young people have become an increasing public health concern.

Suicide remains the second-leading cause of death among Americans ages 15 to 34.

But mental health is about more than the absence of mental illness. My student researchers and I wanted to ask a somewhat different question: What helps young people flourish?

To answer that question, we created a broad measure of well-being that captured more than the lack of mental health problems, such as psychological distress. It also included positive aspects of life, such as having supportive relationships, hobbies and a sense of meaning and purpose.

A range of measures to determine well-being

Our research team analyzed responses from 79,246 college students across the United States and Canada.

We examined 51 aspects of students’ lives, including their substance use, the discrimination they encountered, their financial stress, any sleep problems and different relationship challenges.

We also examined how students spent their free time, whether that meant exercising, studying, socializing, meditating, playing video games or scrolling on social media.

We used statistical methods that allowed us to compare dozens of potential influences on student well-being simultaneously, helping us identify which factors were most strongly associated with flourishing.

Among the dozens of factors we examined, six stood out as the most important and influential.

Time spent with others pays off

The strongest factor connected to student flourishing was remarkably ordinary: spending time with other people. Students who spent more hours socializing with friends, attending student organizations and participating in cultural events tended to report feeling an overall sense of well-being.

The second most important factor surprised us. Students who spent more time on obligations, including paid work and unpaid family responsibilities, also tended to report a greater sense of well-being.

Our results raise an intriguing possibility: Well-being may come not only from leisure and self-care but also from contributing to something larger than oneself.

While problematic substance use, passive screen time and sleep problems tended to compromise well-being, these factors weren’t the biggest detriment. It was difficulty navigating interpersonal relationships, including problems with friends, romantic partners and roommates.

Making friends, maintaining healthy relationships and working through conflicts requires practice, and some of that practice time now competes with communication mediated by screens.

Notably, the contributors to student flourishing were similar among students diagnosed with anxiety or depression and those without these diagnoses. That suggests these everyday experiences may matter across a broad spectrum of mental health.

Helping students thrive

Supporting students’ mental and emotional health is not simply a matter of reducing screen time. It also means making it easier for young people to spend time together in person, whether through clubs, recreation programs, community events or other welcoming spaces.

Counseling and educational programs can likewise help students build friendships, communicate effectively and navigate conflict in healthy ways.

None of this means mental illness can be solved by telling a struggling young person to put down their phone, join a club or get more sleep. Mental health conditions are complex, and people experiencing them need access to effective professional care.

But our findings suggest that helping young people thrive requires more than treating symptoms. It also requires cultivating supportive relationships, healthy sleep and meaningful engagement in work, school and family life.

Roxanne Prichard receives funding from the National Science Foundation.

articles.title: Five ways to look after yourself as winter approaches
articles.author: Andy M Morley, Subject Lead: Psychology & Neuroscience, University of Lancashire
articles.summary: A few small changes to your daily routine can help you cope better during the winter months.
articles.contentHtml:
When the clocks “fall back” in the autumn, it signals the start of the winter months. And, for many, this time change also signals the start of a difficult period – where the cold weather and long nights wear on their mental health.

To help you adjust to the darker evenings, here are our five top tips for easing your way through the winter:

1. Make the most of the daylight

Natural light regulates our body clock – the internal system which influences our sleep quality and alertness. Your body will take time to adjust to the changes, notably the evenings being darker, earlier. This in turn may disrupt your sleep patterns, which might mean grumpier mornings due to a lack of sleep.

Try to make the most of the day’s light by spending time outdoors – even if this is just a walk around the block during your lunch or while on a coffee break. A change of scenery can offer a welcome pause from the pressures of everyday life and help you feel refreshed, particularly if you focus on the greenery around you.

Even if you cannot find time to leave the building, try sitting next by a window to enjoy some natural light and a different perspective on you surroundings.

2. Keep moving

When it’s cold and dark, it’s all too easy to skip your workouts and hunker down inside with a hot drink or favourite snack instead.

But exercise has many benefits for us beyond just the physical ones. It can reduce stress and improve your mental health.

Taking a stroll, visiting the gym or even walking laps around your kitchen table or garden will help you cope with the change in the season. You could even combine exercise with seasonal activities – such as walking to see Halloween decorations or Christmas lights in the local area.

3. Be kind to yourself

It’s perfectly okay to adjust your expectations about your daily accomplishments in the winter months. With less daylight and worsening weather it can be hard to keep to the pace of life you’ve set yourself and enjoyed over the summer months.

Self-compassion supports your wellbeing. This can involve being kind to yourself, recognising the things you have achieved and celebrating the small wins along the way.

You don’t have to make the most of everyday, or be productive all of the time. Find the balance and allow yourself some slower days. And rather than criticising yourself for not completing everything you had lined up for the day, acknowledge what you have achieved. Having this kind of self-compassion is linked with better mental wellbeing.

4. Stay connected to others

When it’s dark, cold and wet, it’s easy to want to prioritise “me time” at the expense of catching up. But making time for your friends and family is key during the winter months. This is because strong social connections are important for good mental health.

Even if it’s just a short chat about a new film you’ve seen or a great book you’ve read, this time spent connecting with loved ones and maintaining these meaningful connections can help to support your mental wellbeing.

5. Enjoy life’s simple pleasures

Make time for the little things in life – whether that’s reading, cooking, listening to music or picking up a hobby you forgot about.

Research on behavioural activation, which involves reconnecting with rewarding and meaningful activities, shows that these kinds of endeavours improve mood – particularly when motivation has fallen.

Planning one “fun” thing to do each day – no matter how big or small – can help ease the darker evenings and colder nights. You can also make the most of the longer evenings by snuggling up under the duvet to watch a box set without feeling you have to make the most of being outside, or enjoy more at-home activities – such as cooking a favourite meal or indulging in seasonal treats.

Looking ahead

If nothing else, remember the shortest day of the year (in the UK at least) is only a few weeks away. After that, the evenings will start to get lighter again.

Looking after your mental health during winter isn’t about forcing yourself to be positive – it’s about finding the small ways that provide you with support, happiness or enable you to connect with other people.

Feeling less energetic during the winter is common, but if you have persistent low mood, a loss of interest in activities, feel hopeless or loss your appetite, seek additional support via the NHS. Self-care is important, but you do not have to manage everything alone.

articles.title: Scientists discover a surprising secret behind the human brain’s wrinkles
articles.summary: Scientists have discovered why common marmosets have unusually small, smooth brains despite starting development much like other primates. The secret lies in subtle changes to brain-building cells that slow neuron production, revealing new clues about how the large, folded human brain evolved.
